title_en: Ying Juanli v. eBay EachNet Network Information Services (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. — dispute over service contract
ruling_gist_en: 1. In an online transaction, where a website providing a trading platform forms an intermediary contract relationship with the parties to the transaction, the website bears the obligations of an intermediary as stipulated in the Contract Law, such as faithfully reporting matters concerning the conclusion of the contract to both parties, and not intentionally concealing important facts related to the contract or providing false information. If these obligations are violated, the website shall bear corresponding legal liability.

full_text_en:
Ying Juanli v. YiBei YiQu Network Information Services (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. — dispute over service contract

【Ruling Summary】

I. In an online transaction, where the website providing the trading platform and the parties to the transaction form a brokerage contract relationship, the website shall bear the obligations of a broker as stipulated in the Contract Law, such as faithfully reporting to both parties matters relating to the conclusion of the contract, and not intentionally concealing material facts relating to the conclusion of the contract or providing false information. If these obligations are breached, the website shall bear corresponding legal liability.

II. Where a party enters into an online sales contract with another person through the website’s trading platform, but does not actually perform that contract; instead, using the personal information of the other party provided by the website, the party contacts the other party by telephone and concludes a new contract that is entirely different from the online sales contract, such new contract is unrelated to the website; and the party suffers economic losses from performing such new contract, the website shall not bear liability for damages.

Plaintiff: Ying Juanli, female, 25 years old, residing at Zhongshan Road, Jiading City, Zhejiang Province.

Defendant: YiBei YiQu Network Information Services (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., domiciled at Guo Shou Jing Road, Zhangjiang High-Tech Park, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Shao Yibo, Chairman of the Company.

The plaintiff, Ying Juanli, filed an action with the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant, YiBei YiQu Network Information Services (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as YiBei YiQu Company), concerning a dispute over a service contract.

The plaintiff, Ying Juanli, alleged: In October 2004, through the defendant's website, the plaintiff successfully bid for a Samsung YP-520H MP3 player offered by a seller with the screen name “我想有个家1”. On October 21, 2004, the plaintiff received the transaction confirmation from the defendant. The plaintiff then contacted the seller using the information provided by the defendant. On October 22, 2004, the plaintiff remitted the payment of RMB 1,092 for the MP3 player to the seller “我想有个家1” through the Agricultural Bank of China in Jiaxing City. Several days after remitting the payment, the plaintiff did not receive the MP3 player. On November 3, 2004, the plaintiff formally faxed a complaint to the defendant, requesting the defendant's assistance in recovering the payment. On November 24, 2004, the plaintiff faxed a legal letter to the defendant, demanding that the defendant assume liability, but the defendant did not give a direct response. The plaintiff argued that the defendant, as an online trading platform, should bear corresponding legal liability in this case; the disclaimer clause in the defendant's registration agreement is invalid; and the defendant's transaction rules have serious security flaws, and the defendant failed to meet its “duty of care.” The plaintiff requested a judgment ordering the defendant to refund double the amount of the payment already made by the plaintiff, totaling RMB 2,184.

The defendant, YiBei YiQu Company, argued: The defendant provides an online information exchange platform and does not participate in transactions. Before registering as a user of the defendant, the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, should have carefully read the defendant's registration agreement and registered as a user only after accepting the terms thereof. The disclaimer clause in the registration agreement, as part of the contract, reflects the true intent of both parties and has legal effect. The plaintiff successfully bid for the MP3 player offered by the seller with the screen name “我想有个家1” and the online name Zhang Xu, at a “buy-it-now” price of RMB 1 per unit. However, after contacting the seller using the telephone number provided by the defendant, the plaintiff actually concluded the transaction at a price of RMB 156 per unit, and when the plaintiff learned that the seller's bank account name was He Jinhai, not Zhang Xu, the plaintiff nevertheless remitted the payment. The resulting losses should be borne by the plaintiff. The defendant requested a judgment rejecting the plaintiff's claims.

The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts upon trial:

The eBay EachNet Shopping Network (hereinafter referred to as EachNet) is a transaction website operated by the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company. On August 10, 2004, the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, read and accepted EachNet’s User Agreement and registered as a user of EachNet. The User Agreement stipulates that EachNet does not participate in actual transactions, and EachNet disclaims liability in the event of disputes between buyers and sellers. In October 2004, through EachNet, the plaintiff successfully bid for a Samsung YP-520H MP3 player offered by a registered seller with the screen name “我想有个家1”. On October 21, 2004, the plaintiff successfully bid at a “buy-it-now” price of RMB 1 per unit for the Samsung YP-520H MP3 player and received the transaction confirmation from EachNet. Through EachNet, the plaintiff learned that the item provider was Zhang Xu, a seller in Tianjin (a third party unrelated to this case), and also obtained Zhang Xu’s telephone number and email address. According to the plaintiff’s statement, after contacting Zhang Xu by telephone, the plaintiff agreed that Zhang Xu would sell seven Samsung YP-520H MP3 players to the plaintiff at a price of RMB 156 per unit, with the method of performance being payment before delivery, and the payment to be remitted to a bank account designated by Zhang Xu, which was in the name of another third party, He Jinhai, with account number 9559980020128963913 at the Agricultural Bank of China. On October 22, 2004, using the bank account name and number provided by Zhang Xu, the plaintiff remitted the full payment of RMB 1,092 for the seven Samsung YP-520H MP3 players through the Agricultural Bank of China to account number 9559980020128963913 in the name of He Jinhai. After remitting the payment, the plaintiff never received the Samsung YP-520H MP3 players as agreed. On November 3, 2004, the plaintiff sent a complaint letter to the defendant, requesting that the defendant contact Zhang Xu as soon as possible and provide a feasible solution, and that Zhang Xu at least refund the full payment. The plaintiff also requested that the defendant impose severe sanctions on Zhang Xu, suggesting that Zhang Xu be removed from EachNet, and that the matter of Zhang Xu trading under another person's name be reported to the Tianjin public security authorities. On November 24, 2004, the plaintiff sent another letter to the defendant, stating that the plaintiff did not accept the defendant's response and demanded that the defendant refund double the full payment already made by the plaintiff, totaling RMB 2,184. The defendant refused.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: the online transaction confirmation from EachNet provided by the plaintiff, Ying Juanli; the receipt slip for the bank deposit at the Agricultural Bank of China; the complaint letter and legal letter; as well as the EachNet User Agreement provided by the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company; the plaintiff’s registration information on EachNet; the page for the item purchased by the plaintiff at the “buy-it-now” price; the plaintiff’s complaint letter and attachments; and the defendant’s reply letter. The above evidence was examined in court and confirmed by the court.

The issue in dispute in this case is: whether the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company, should be liable for the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, having paid the purchase price but failing to receive the ordered Samsung YP-520H MP3 players as agreed.

The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai held:

A contract established in accordance with law is protected by law and is binding on all parties to the contract. However, in this case, the sales contract between the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, and the third party, Zhang Xu, is unrelated to the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company. Ying Juanli paid the purchase price but failed to receive the ordered Samsung YP-520H MP3 players as agreed; YiBei YiQu Company should not bear liability for this.

First, in online transactions, a website, as an interactive computer service provider, on the one hand provides a paid information platform for online sellers to display their goods and prices (specifically manifested by the online seller’s registration behavior on the network), and on the other hand provides buyers with information about the seller and the goods (specifically manifested by the buyer’s registration behavior on the network), and confirms whether a transaction is concluded based on the mutual agreement of both parties. If a transaction is concluded, the website sends a transaction confirmation and the other party’s contact information to both parties, and collects corresponding fees from the seller. Specifically in this case, the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company, provided intermediary services for concluding contracts to the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, and the third party, Zhang Xu, and collected fees from Zhang Xu. Therefore, a brokerage contract relationship existed between the defendant and the plaintiff, as well as between the defendant and Zhang Xu. Accordingly, the defendant’s obligation in this case should be the obligations of a broker as stipulated in the Contract Law, such as faithfully reporting to the plaintiff matters relating to the conclusion of the contract, and not intentionally concealing material facts relating to the conclusion of the contract or providing false information. If these obligations are breached, the defendant should bear liability for breach of contract. In this case, the defendant did not breach the above obligations.

Second, there were actually two separate contractual relationships between the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, and the third party, Zhang Xu. One was an online sales contract relationship. Zhang Xu’s provision of information on available goods for sale on the website could be regarded as an invitation to offer; the plaintiff’s willingness to bid at a “buy-it-now” price of RMB 1 per unit for the Samsung YP-520H MP3 player could be regarded as an offer. Pursuant to the agreement between the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company, and Zhang Xu, the defendant’s sending of the transaction confirmation to the plaintiff on behalf of Zhang Xu could be regarded as Zhang Xu’s acceptance. At that point, the online sales contract relationship between the plaintiff and Zhang Xu was established. The other was a traditional sales contract relationship established between the plaintiff and Zhang Xu by telephone. Using Zhang Xu’s contact information provided by the defendant, the plaintiff contacted Zhang Xu by telephone and agreed that Zhang Xu would sell seven Samsung YP-520H MP3 players to the plaintiff at a price of RMB 156 per unit, and agreed on the method of performance and payment. The two thus established another sales contract relationship. The conclusion of this contract relationship did not follow the relevant provisions of the User Agreement separately agreed between each contracting party and the defendant, and was not directly related to the defendant. The purpose of the defendant providing Zhang Xu’s contact information to the plaintiff was to facilitate the actual performance of the previous online sales contract, not for the plaintiff and Zhang Xu to engage in other transactions.

Third, in determining whether the defendant, YiBei YiQu Company, should bear civil liability for the plaintiff, Ying Juanli, having paid the purchase price but failing to receive the ordered Samsung YP-520H MP3 players as agreed, the factual basis should be whether the defendant fulfilled its relevant review obligations and whether it was at fault in providing the personal information of the third party, Zhang Xu. According to the facts of this case, before registering as a user of the defendant, all netizens are required to read the defendant’s User Agreement in detail and can only successfully register after accepting all terms of the agreement. Registration requires inputting personal information such as personal ID number, address, and telephone number. The defendant provides services to registrants only after verifying their personal information with the public security authorities. The plaintiff and Zhang Xu both went through the above registration process. It should be held that the defendant fulfilled its obligations in reviewing Zhang Xu’s personal information and was not at fault. In this case, although the plaintiff, through the defendant, reached a sales contract with Zhang Xu for the purchase of a Samsung YP-520H MP3 player at RMB 1, the dispute in this case did not arise from that online transaction; rather, it arose from another sales contract concluded between the plaintiff and Zhang Xu by telephone, for the purchase of seven Samsung YP-520H MP3 players at a price of RMB 156 per unit. In the course of this transaction, the plaintiff, relying solely on Zhang Xu’s personal information provided by the defendant and without further verification, entered into the contract, and without receiving the goods from the other party or requesting any security, remitted the payment in advance to a bank account of another third party, He Jinhai, designated by the other party, thereby incurring economic losses. It is evident that it was the plaintiff’s own lack of care in the process of concluding and performing the contract that led to being deceived. For these consequences, the plaintiff should bear responsibility. In this litigation, the plaintiff did not provide any evidence that the personal information of Zhang Xu provided by the defendant was untrue or false, nor did the plaintiff provide any evidence that the latter transaction was carried out through the online trading platform provided by the defendant. Therefore, the defendant had no fault with respect to the plaintiff’s losses, and the defendant never received the payment made by the plaintiff. Consequently, the defendant should not bear liability for compensation for the plaintiff’s losses.

Accordingly, the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai, in accordance with Articles 8, 52, and 53 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

The plaintiff’s claims are dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 97 shall be borne by the plaintiff, Ying Juanli.

After the judgment of first instance was rendered, neither party filed an appeal within the statutory period, and the judgment of first instance took legal effect.
